_README: Rule table for spectral fault signatures. Each rule lists the orders of
running speed it expects, with a role:
dominant      must be present AND be the largest matched peak
required      must be present
supporting    adds evidence when present, costs nothing when absent
contradicting subtracts evidence when present
Missing a dominant or required order disqualifies the rule outright. That
is deliberate: 'unbalance' with no 1x peak is not a weak unbalance case,
it is not unbalance.
Order references beginning with '@' are resolved from machine context at
match time - @bpfo/@bpfi/@bsf/@bsf2x/@ftf from bearing geometry, @gmf from
gear teeth, @vane_pass / @blade_pass from impeller geometry, @line_2x from
supply frequency, @belt from sheave geometry. A rule whose reference
cannot be resolved is skipped rather than guessed at, so a machine with no
gearbox never gets a gear-mesh hypothesis.
tol_order is absolute (in orders); tol_pct is relative. Bearing
frequencies use tol_pct because rolling elements slip by 1-2%, so measured
defect frequencies sit slightly below the kinematic values.
This table ranks. It does not explain - the graph attaches a textbook
passage per top hypothesis using query_hint.

unbalance.name: Unbalance
unbalance.mechanism: A rotating mass eccentricity produces a once-per-revolution centrifugal force, so energy concentrates at 1x and is predominantly radial.
confirming_checks: Phase is stable and repeatable at 1x.
Horizontal and vertical phase differ by roughly 90 degrees on the same bearing.
Amplitude rises with the square of speed.
unbalance.query_hint: unbalance vibration 1x running speed radial phase diagnosis rotor

misalignment_parallel.name: Parallel (offset) misalignment
misalignment_parallel.mechanism: Offset shaft centrelines load the coupling twice per revolution, so 2x radial dominates while 1x remains present.
confirming_checks: Phase shifts about 180 degrees across the coupling in the radial direction.
2x amplitude is often more than half of 1x.
misalignment_parallel.query_hint: parallel offset misalignment 2x running speed coupling radial vibration diagnosis

misalignment_angular.name: Angular misalignment
misalignment_angular.mechanism: Angled shaft centrelines bend the coupling once and twice per revolution along the shaft axis, so high 1x and 2x appear axially.
confirming_checks: Axial amplitude is comparable to or greater than radial.
Phase shifts about 180 degrees across the coupling in the axial direction.
misalignment_angular.query_hint: angular misalignment axial vibration 1x 2x coupling phase shift diagnosis

bent_shaft.name: Bent shaft
bent_shaft.mechanism: A bowed rotor produces a once-per-revolution axial displacement; the bend location determines whether 1x or 2x axial dominates.
confirming_checks: High axial vibration at 1x.
Axial phase differs by about 180 degrees across the rotor.
Distinguish from angular misalignment by checking runout with a dial indicator.
bent_shaft.query_hint: bent shaft bowed rotor axial vibration 1x phase diagnosis

mechanical_looseness.name: Mechanical looseness
mechanical_looseness.mechanism: A loose joint or worn fit lets the rotor move nonlinearly, clipping the response and generating half-order subharmonics plus a long harmonic series.
confirming_checks: Raised noise floor across the spectrum.
Directional amplitude: often much higher in one radial direction.
Time waveform shows truncation or impacting.
mechanical_looseness.query_hint: mechanical looseness subharmonic half order harmonics raised noise floor vibration diagnosis

structural_looseness.name: Structural looseness / soft foot
structural_looseness.mechanism: Loose hold-down bolts or a soft foot let the machine rock on its base, amplifying 1x with harmonics, usually strongest vertically.
confirming_checks: Amplitude drops sharply when hold-down bolts are tightened.
Phase differs across the foot / base / foundation joint.
Check for soft foot with a feeler gauge or by loosening one foot at a time.
structural_looseness.query_hint: structural looseness soft foot base foundation vibration 1x harmonics diagnosis

bearing_outer_race.name: Rolling-element bearing — outer race defect
bearing_outer_race.mechanism: Each rolling element striking a defect on the stationary outer race produces an impact at BPFO. Because the defect stays in the load zone, the amplitude is steady and sidebands are usually weak.
confirming_checks: Peaks are non-synchronous — not integer multiples of running speed.
Envelope (demodulated) spectrum shows BPFO far more clearly than the raw spectrum.
Crest factor and kurtosis of the time waveform are elevated.
bearing_outer_race.query_hint: ball pass frequency outer race BPFO bearing defect envelope spectrum diagnosis

bearing_inner_race.name: Rolling-element bearing — inner race defect
bearing_inner_race.mechanism: The inner race defect rotates through the load zone once per revolution, so the BPFI impacts are amplitude-modulated at running speed — producing 1x sidebands around BPFI.
confirming_checks: Sidebands spaced at 1x running speed around BPFI. This is the distinguishing feature versus an outer race defect.
Envelope spectrum shows BPFI plus its 1x sidebands.
bearing_inner_race.query_hint: ball pass frequency inner race BPFI sidebands running speed bearing defect diagnosis

bearing_ball_defect.name: Rolling-element bearing — rolling element defect
bearing_ball_defect.mechanism: A defect on a rolling element strikes both races once per element revolution, so 2xBSF usually dominates over BSF. The element passes through the load zone at cage rate, modulating the impacts at FTF.
confirming_checks: Sidebands spaced at cage frequency (FTF) around 2xBSF.
2xBSF is normally stronger than BSF itself.
bearing_ball_defect.query_hint: ball spin frequency BSF rolling element defect cage sidebands bearing diagnosis

bearing_cage.name: Rolling-element bearing — cage damage
bearing_cage.mechanism: A damaged or worn cage produces a low-frequency component at the fundamental train frequency, typically 0.35-0.45x running speed. Rarely appears alone — usually accompanies advanced element or race damage.
confirming_checks: FTF sits below 0.5x, distinguishing it from looseness subharmonics at exactly 0.5x.
Often modulates other bearing frequencies rather than appearing as a strong discrete peak.
bearing_cage.query_hint: fundamental train frequency FTF cage defect bearing diagnosis

gear_mesh.name: Gear mesh / gear tooth defect
gear_mesh.mechanism: Teeth mesh at N_teeth x shaft rate. A localised tooth defect modulates the mesh once per revolution of the shaft carrying it, so the sideband spacing identifies which gear is faulty.
confirming_checks: Sideband spacing equals the running speed of the FAULTY gear's shaft — this is how you tell which gear it is.
Rising sideband energy matters more than rising GMF amplitude alone.
Time waveform shows a once-per-revolution impact.
gear_mesh.query_hint: gear mesh frequency GMF sidebands tooth defect gearbox vibration diagnosis

blade_vane_pass.name: Blade / vane pass
blade_vane_pass.mechanism: Each blade or vane passing the cutwater or a stationary diffuser produces a pressure pulse at N x shaft rate. Present on every machine of this type; only a rise above baseline is a fault.
confirming_checks: A moderate vane-pass peak is normal for a pump or fan — compare against the baseline trend, not against zero.
A large rise suggests increased clearance, cavitation, flow restriction, or an eroded impeller.
Cavitation adds broadband random energy at high frequency, unlike a clean vane-pass peak.
blade_vane_pass.query_hint: blade pass vane pass frequency pump fan impeller vibration diagnosis cavitation

electrical.name: Electrical fault
electrical.mechanism: Magnetic forces in an induction machine act twice per supply cycle, so an electrical asymmetry — rotor bar, stator eccentricity, unbalanced supply — shows at twice line frequency, not at a multiple of shaft speed.
confirming_checks: The peak sits at exactly 2x line frequency (100 Hz on 50 Hz supply, 120 Hz on 60 Hz), NOT at a running-speed order.
Decisive test: the peak disappears instantly on power-off, whereas mechanical vibration coasts down with speed.
Pole-pass sidebands around 1x indicate broken rotor bars.
electrical.query_hint: electrical fault twice line frequency rotor bar pole pass sidebands motor vibration diagnosis

oil_whirl.name: Oil whirl (journal bearing instability)
oil_whirl.mechanism: In a lightly loaded journal bearing the oil wedge drags the shaft around at slightly less than half shaft speed, producing a subsynchronous peak at 0.38-0.48x.
confirming_checks: Applies only to fluid-film (journal / sleeve) bearings — not to rolling-element bearings.
The peak tracks speed at a constant fraction. If it locks at a fixed frequency as speed rises, it has become oil whip.
Orbit plot shows a forward precessing loop.
oil_whirl.query_hint: oil whirl whip journal bearing subsynchronous 0.43x instability orbit diagnosis

belt_drive.name: Belt drive fault
belt_drive.mechanism: A defect in the belt itself passes each sheave once per belt revolution, producing a subsynchronous belt frequency and its harmonics.
confirming_checks: Belt frequency is subsynchronous — below 1x on both sheaves.
2x belt frequency is often the largest of the series.
Strobe the belt to see the defect directly.
belt_drive.query_hint: belt frequency sheave pulley defect harmonics vibration diagnosis

cavitation.name: Cavitation

features.statement: The spectrum is close to featureless -- energy spread evenly rather than concentrated in lines, which is random excitation rather than rotation
Almost none of the energy sits in discrete harmonics, which is what separates cavitation from every rotational fault
There is enough signal for the broadband energy to mean something -- a stopped machine also has a featureless spectrum

The waveform is not impulsive. This is the discriminator that matters most: a bearing defect also lifts the high-frequency floor and also looks broadband, and the only thing separating it from cavitation is that a defect strikes repeatedly while collapsing bubbles do not. Left as merely supporting, a bearing fault with a crest factor of 9 still scored 0.84 as cavitation

cavitation.mechanism: Low suction pressure lets vapour bubbles form and then collapse violently against the impeller. Each collapse is an independent impact, so the energy is random and broadband rather than tied to any rotational frequency -- which is why cavitation has no peak to find and is recognised by the absence of one.
confirming_checks: Listen at the pump: cavitation sounds like gravel passing through it.
Check suction conditions first -- strainers, valve position, level, and net positive suction head.
Throttling the discharge should change the noise; a bearing fault will not care.
Cavitation erodes impellers, so a long-running case usually shows as a rising vane-pass amplitude as well.
On a gateway whose signal sits at the converter's own floor, a dead channel and a cavitating pump both produce a featureless spectrum. Check the capture has real amplitude before acting on this.
cavitation.query_hint: cavitation pump broadband noise suction NPSH vibration diagnosis

rotor_bar.name: Rotor bar defect
rotor_bar.mechanism: A cracked or broken rotor bar carries no current, so the rotor's magnetic field becomes asymmetric and the torque pulses once per pole pass. That modulates running speed, putting sidebands at running speed plus and minus the pole-pass frequency -- and pole pass is slip times the pole count, so the spacing is tiny and needs a long record to resolve.
confirming_checks: Both sidebands should be present and roughly symmetric about running speed; one alone is more often a nearby unrelated peak.
Confirm the pole count and measure the actual speed; the sideband spacing is derived from slip and is wrong if either is guessed.
Current signature analysis is the definitive test and is cheaper than dismantling the motor.
The sidebands grow with load, because slip does.
rotor_bar.query_hint: rotor bar defect pole pass sideband slip motor current signature analysis vibration
